results.text: From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries. A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements. The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment. “It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.” One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785. Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said.

To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

results.text: Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles. This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce.

So, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of? Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true. • Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author of The 21st Century Brain (Torva). results.text: up.” Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth. In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements. Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain.

The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check. The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way. MacLean conducted dissections of living creatures to try to prove his theory, but the results, and his interpretations of them, have since been largely discredited. For example, it’s now accepted that many reptiles do actually possess the “mammalian” limbic system, while all mammals exhibit “neomammalian” features previously thought to be unique to “higher” ones like us.

Alongside these anatomical observations, there’s the behavioural data too, with many “lower” animals good at problem solving, responding and learning via emotion, and communicating in complex ways. As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. For a start, mammals and reptiles split early in evolutionary terms. Whilst it is true that more primitive functions in our brains evolved earlier in the course of life on Earth, this view of three separate brain systems driving our basic instincts, emotions and logic respectively does not stack up.” Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth.

Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. results.text: We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega. The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August. As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two. Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus. In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

results.text: This week offers one of the better opportunities of the year to catch a glimpse of the solar system’s innermost world. Trapped in its small orbit, Mercury never strays far from the sun, meaning it is usually lost to the light of dawn or dusk. On Sunday, however, the planet reached its greatest western elongation, meaning it appeared at its greatest apparent distance from the sun in the morning sky. The next few mornings offer one of the best opportunities this year for catching a glimpse of the planet as it steadily brightens, improving the contrast with the gathering dawn. An early start and an unobstructed view towards the east-north-east will be essential to making the sighting. The chart shows the view looking in this direction from London at 04.30 BST on Tuesday. If your line of sight is free from obstructions, the planet will become visible about a handspan above the horizon some time between 04.30 and 05.00. Binoculars can help, but exercise caution: sunrise on Tuesday from London occurs at 05.28, so stop using binoculars well before this time to protect your eyesight. As a bonus, Mars will be much easier to spot, higher and to the east.

results.text: A near total lunar eclipse will be visible across large swathes of North and South America on Thursday night with millions of people expected to be able to see one of nature’s marvels. Lunar eclipses occur when Earth moves between the sun and the moon and its shadow is cast on to the lunar surface. In Thursday night’s event 96% of the moon will be darkened by the Earth’s shadow at its peak moment. The eclipse will be one known as a “blood moon”, as the Earth’s shadow will appear to be reddish due to the way sunlight is scattered by the Earth’s atmosphere. It will mainly be visible in the Americas but also in a few parts of Europe and Africa. It will begin about 9.23pm EST, peaking around 10.33pm EST. Earlier this month, millions of people across Europe watched a more dramatic solar eclipse where the moon blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness.

results.text: The September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September. It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky. As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal. This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox. In the UK, the date on which day and night come closest to being equal will be a couple of days later, around 25 September.

results.text: From the moment scientists spotted plumes of water erupting from Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, it became the most tantalising place in the solar system to search for life beyond Earth. Now the case is even more compelling after researchers found that organisms that live in deep-sea waters off Japan can survive the harsh conditions expected in the briny ocean that lurks beneath Enceladus’s icy crust. The microbes, which thrive near hydrothermal vents on the seafloor by converting hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, survived in a brine that mimicked the Saturnian moon’s ocean. The work suggests the distant world may be habitable, if not exactly hospitable, to at least some forms of life. “If we use the cellular definition of life that we understand on Earth today, the experiments tell us that if this organism, or something similar to it, was on Enceladus, there’s a good chance it could survive,” said William Orsi, a professor of geomicrobiology at Ludwig-Maximilian University in Munich. Saturn has more moons than any other planet in the solar system, with nearly 300 known to orbit the gas giant.

The September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September. It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky. As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal. This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox. In the UK, the date on which day and night come closest to being equal will be a couple of days later, around 25 September.

results.text: A tiny alga has helped show how memories, feelings and behaviour form in our brains, in research by three scientists awarded the Nobel prize for physiology or medicine this month. Chlamydomonas is a one-celled alga that swims towards light using a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, remarkably similar to the rhodopsin in our eyes. When the channelrhodopsin detects light, electrically charged ions rush into the cell from outside, triggering an electrical signal incredibly fast that tells the alga to move with its hair-like motor. In the research, the gene for the Chlamydomonas channelrhodopsin was transferred into living animal brain cells and flashes of light were used to switch individual neurons on or off, helping pinpoint the exact circuits in the brain that control behaviour, feelings, memories, movements, waking and sleeping, and other bodily functions. It could even switch on how mice gather their young in a nest or groom them. This technique is being used to investigate disorders such as depression, anxiety and Parkinson’s disease, and is being tested to partially restore vision in people with diseases of the retina.

In 1996, the government’s expert advisory body, the Farm Animal Welfare Council – now called the Animal Welfare Committee – suggested there should be legislation governing the slaughter of farmed fish. The committee returned to the issue in 2014 and again in 2024. On the latter occasion it urged governments across the UK to legislate for fish to be stunned before slaughter, and for inspection systems to be put in place to enforce those standards.

In its Animal Welfare Strategy for England, published in December 2025, the government committed to introducing humane slaughter requirements for farmed fish but draft legislation has yet to be published.

Penny said: “For 30 years, people in power have known that farmed fish need legal protection when they are slaughtered, yet for 30 years decisionmakers have failed to act.”

citation.title: Lack of inspections at fish slaughterhouses a ‘disgrace’, says Animal Equality UK

results.text:
Up to 77m fish are slaughtered each year in the UK but there are no routine or mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses in England and Wales, it can be revealed.

Concerns within government about the way fish are slaughtered date back decades but all of the official bodies responsible for animal welfare and food standards in England and Wales said they do not undertake regular inspections.

When Animal Equality UK contacted the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), it referred the charity to the Fish Health Inspectorate (FHI). In response to a previous inquiry, the APHA had said it does not carry out mandatory inspections of fish slaughterhouses and suggested contacting the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Both the FSA and the FHI told Animal Equality UK that they did not carry out routine or mandatory inspections.

Abigail Penny, the executive director of Animal Equality UK, said: “Fish are thinking, feeling beings, capable of pain. It is a disgrace that not a single government agency will take responsibility for checking on their welfare at slaughter. This is a huge blindspot, and it leaves these animals all the more vulnerable behind closed doors.”

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.

The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.

Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.

The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.

Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

results.text:
Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, it was small – even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.

Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, may stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?

“People have locked in,” says Metzger. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognise that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
Twenty years ago, Pluto got demoted. After a vote by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in August 2006, Pluto was relegated from major planet to dwarf planet status. Our solar system dropped from nine planets to eight. At the time, many scientists were unhappy with the decision. Two decades on, the debate is, if anything, even more polarised.

“The definition of a planet they created, you can’t use it at all,” says Philip Metzger, the director of the Stephen W Hawking Centre for Microgravity Research and Education at the University of Central Florida. “It makes the definition of a planet completely non-useful in science.”

Metzger is one of a number of scientists and lay people who consider Pluto’s demotion a big mistake.

For some, Pluto’s downgraded status is the source of their affection for the ex-planet. “Pluto represents the underdog that so many people root for, the small kid on the block that is being picked on,” says Kevin Schindler, historian at the Lowell Observatory in Arizona, where Pluto was discovered in 1930.

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
The event that sparked the IAU’s 2006 vote was the discovery of a distant celestial body that would come to be called Eris. Eris was out in the Kuiper Belt, beyond Neptune – where Pluto also resides. It was roughly the same size as Pluto (less volume, but more mass). If Pluto was a planet, the argument went, then so was Eris. And if Eris wasn’t a planet, how could Pluto continue to be one?

Eris and Pluto were by no means alone in the Kuiper Belt. Other smaller bodies were discovered around the same time, including Haumea, Makemake and Sedna. Were these also planets? There were likely many more similar objects still to be found. How would schoolchildren manage a planetary roster that might number in the hundreds?

In search of a solution, the IAU came up with a three-point definition of a planet: it must orbit the Sun; it must have sufficient mass to pull itself into a round shape; and it must have “cleared its neighbourhood” – meaning it must gravitationally dominate the area in which it orbits. Nothing beyond Neptune that we knew about qualified; Pluto was out.

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
Pluto’s demotion created two opposing scientific teams: the so-called geophysical camp, which believes the physical properties of a celestial body should count toward its planethood; and the dynamicists, who are more concerned with the position a body occupies, its surroundings and its direction of travel. You could characterise the split as planetary scientists v astronomers. Many planetary scientists, including Metzger, simply do not use the IAU definition.

When the New Horizons spacecraft made its flyby of Pluto in 2015, the geophysical camp seized what it saw as an advantage. Pluto definitely had the geophysical makings of a planet, they maintained. It had mountains, evidence of recent geological activity, and water ice hills floating on frozen nitrogen. It might even be able to support life. How could that not be a planet?

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

results.text:
For Metzger, the planetary definition excluding Pluto is based on an outmoded notion of the solar system. “They were creating a reactionary view towards an orderly cosmos, rather than the more modern scientific view where it’s chaotic,” he says. “The second problem was that I think they misread the room. The public of today is not the public of the 1800s. They’re perfectly happy understanding a dynamic, chaotic cosmos, and we missed the opportunity to teach that.”

Pluto’s nature has always been elusive. In 1915, the astronomer Percival Lowell published calculations based on peculiarities in the orbits of Uranus and Neptune, predicting the existence of a new, ninth planet, which he called Planet X, with a mass somewhere between Earth’s and Neptune’s. In 1930, the long search for Planet X bore fruit: the new body, discovered at the observatory that bore Lowell’s name, was christened Pluto.

citation.title: Forbidden planet: was Pluto’s 2006 demotion a big mistake?

Gradually, however, it became clear that whatever Pluto was, it wasn’t Planet X. It didn’t seem anywhere near large enough to account for irregularities in Neptune’s orbit. Scientists offered theories to explain why Pluto looked so small, but the truth was, it was small – even smaller than the moon. Only in 1992 did we learn that Lowell’s calculations were based on an overestimation of Neptune’s mass. There was no Planet X.

Pluto’s reputation as an underdog, the picked-on kid, may stem from the 2006 vote, but one could argue it was punching above its weight for years. How would they have voted on Pluto’s planetary status if they had known the truth in 1930? And will it take another vote to satisfy Pluto’s defenders?

“People have locked in,” says Metzger. “We would have a less useful vote today than we did back in the 2006 timeframe. So we don’t want another vote. What we want is for people to recognise that voting was a mistake, and we’re not going to do that any more. We’re going to go back to the scientific method.”

We are on the hunt for another small, northern summer constellation this week: Sagitta, the arrow. Although it consists of just a handful of faint stars, Sagitta’s distinctive shape (it really does look like an arrow) makes it easy to identify against a dark sky.

The chart shows the view looking up towards the zenith while facing south from London at 22.30 BST on Monday.

Sagitta can be found about partway along the imaginary line connecting Vega and Altair, which make up the summer triangle with Deneb.

Although it is the third-smallest constellation in the sky, Sagitta has been recognised since ancient times. The 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy placed it on his list of 48 constellations published in The Almagest.

There are a number of stories from Greek mythology that could be attributed to the arrow. It could be the one fired by Hercules to kill the eagle tormenting Prometheus, or it could be one of Cupid’s famous arrows.

Observers in the southern hemisphere can also see Sagitta during August, although it appears lower in the northern sky than it does from the UK.

This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon.

The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October.

Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda.

The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs. Notice that the horse appears upside down.

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.

The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.

Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.

The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.

Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

citation.title: Starwatch: Tracking down the faint stars of Pisces

We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega.

The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August.

As the fifth-brightest star in the night sky, Vega forms one corner of the summer triangle, with Deneb in Cygnus, the Swan, and Altair in Aquila, the Eagle, marking the other two.

Having located Vega, the rest of the constellation is easy to trace even though the stars are much fainter. One of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations, Lyra has the distinction of being a star pattern that actually looks like the figure it is named after. It represents the harp played by the Greek poet Orpheus.

In Greek mythology, Orpheus played such beautiful music that he could charm wild animals, move rocks and even influence the gods. Becoming one of the Argonauts, Orpheus’s music protected the rest of the crew from the beguiling call of the Sirens.

The red planet, Mars, sails through the beautiful cluster of stars known as the Beehive this week. Catalogued as Messier 44, the cluster lies in the constellation Cancer. It has been known since antiquity, when its hazy appearance earned it the Latin name Praesepe, meaning a manger or crib.

Although it is one of the brightest star clusters in the night sky, it can be surprisingly difficult to locate because Cancer contains no bright stars to guide the eye towards it. Thankfully, this week Mars acts as the signpost.

The chart shows the view looking east from London at 0200 BST on 13 October. Mars will appear as a moderately bright, distinctly red-looking object. Once you have Mars in your sights, look carefully around the planet. From a dark location, the Beehive will appear as a faint, misty patch very close to Mars.

Light pollution will make the cluster much harder to see, and wherever you are observing, make sure you allow sufficient time for your eyes to adjust to the dark. This can take about 20 minutes, so resist the temptation to look at the bright screen of your phone.

citation.title: Starwatch: Mars signposts the beautiful Beehive cluster

The storms left behind a sky ribboned with dark clouds. Some team members stood outside the trucks and applauded its beauty, lifting their phones for photographs. Wurman and Kosiba were not among them. They were already studying the models, deciding where the team should spend the night to be best positioned for morning.

***

Tornadoes offer enough spectacle to draw film-makers, thrill-seekers, and carloads of chasers with cameras. But scientists who chase for data need more than drama. They need geometry: an open horizon, a road in and a road out, a storm that forms where the instruments can reach it.

Even when everything lines up, a mobile radar crew can spend weeks following one promising storm after another, only to watch each weaken and dissolve before the instruments capture the measurements they came for.

Why do they keep doing it?

For data analyst Paul Robinson, the pull started with an image on television: Dorothy clutching Toto, calling for Auntie Em as a black twister writhed in the distance.

This week we will track down Pisces, the fishes. Despite being one of the largest zodiacal constellations, it can be surprisingly difficult to identify because it contains no bright stars.

The chart shows the view looking east from London at 10pm on Monday. As the week progresses, the bright waning moon will rise later and later in the evening, allowing the faint stars of Pisces to be more easily seen.

Start by finding the Great Square of Pegasus. Look below its southern edge for a small, faint ring of stars. This is the Circlet of Pisces. Seven stars make up the pattern, although you will not see them all from a semi-urban location.

The circlet represents one of the two fish. From here, a long string of faint stars heads to Alrescha, an Arabic name meaning “the cord”. Another string leads to the second fish, forming a V-shape of stars.

Pisces is one of the second-century astronomer Ptolemy’s original 48 constellations. In Greek mythology, the fishes were associated with Aphrodite and her son Eros, who escaped the monster Typhon by taking the form of fish. They tied themselves together so they would not become separated.

This week we will track down Pegasus, one of the most distinctive constellations in the autumn sky. Pegasus was one of the 48 constellations listed by Ptolemy in the second century. In Greek mythology, it represents the magnificent winged horse ridden by the hero Bellerophon.

The easiest part of the constellation to recognise is the Great Square of Pegasus, a large pattern of four moderately bright stars. The chart shows the view looking high in the southern sky from London at 10pm on 26 October.

Three of these stars, Markab, Scheat and Algenib, belong to Pegasus. The fourth, Alpheratz, is actually part of the neighbouring constellation Andromeda. Historically, Alpheratz was considered to belong to both constellations, but when the official boundaries of the 88 modern constellations were established, it ended up in Andromeda.

The Great Square is the body of Pegasus. From Markab, follow a curving line of stars towards Enif (whose name means nose in Arabic) to trace the horse’s neck and head. Other lines of stars extending from the Square represent the horse’s front legs. Notice that the horse appears upside down.

To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island.

This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history.

A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. High above the Dead Sea’s south-eastern shore, pilgrims once climbed to a cave they believed had sheltered Lot after he fled the destruction of Sodom. For centuries the site survived in Christian memory alone, visited by occasional pilgrims such as St Stephen the Sabaite, until the Greek archaeologist Konstantinos Politis, who has died aged 67 following a series of strokes, began excavating in 1988.

He uncovered a Byzantine basilica built over the mouth of the cave, its floors still adorned with mosaics laid in the sixth and seventh centuries CE. The discovery, at Deir ’Ain ’Abata, gave physical form to one of the Bible’s most vivid stories and set the course for a career spent excavating and protecting the archaeology of Jordan’s Dead Sea shore.

Dino, as Politis was widely known, excavated the Sanctuary of Lot over seven seasons between 1988 and 1996. The site had been identified by an archaeological survey in 1986 as matching a sanctuary depicted on the famous sixth-century mosaic map at Madaba in Jordan, whose location had eluded archaeologists for more than a century.

results.text:
Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west.

In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded by Saint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say.

To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland – it’s extraordinary,” he said.

results.text:
Born in Kozani, Greece, Dino was the son of Demetrios Politis, an officer in the Greek army, and Christine (nee Biller), a schoolteacher. He was educated in Greece, the US, Belgium and Britain, completing an MA at the Institute of Archaeology, University of London, in 1984 and a PhD in archaeology at the University of Ioannina in 2004.

He first went to Jordan in 1984, working with Alison Betts and Svend Helms at Tell Umm Hammad esh-Sharqiya in the north Jordan valley, and in 1985 joined the British Museum’s excavations at Tell es-Sa’idiyeh, led by Jonathan Tubb. In 1988 he joined the British Museum as a special assistant in the department then known as Medieval and Later Antiquities, which supported his early excavations in Jordan. He also joined the museum’s excavations at Ras al-Hadd in Oman, and remained at the British Museum until 2006.

From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries.

A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements.

The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment.

“It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.”

One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785.

Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said. “That would have been an unusual thing to talk about back then.”

citation.title: Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

But there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.

Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.

The accelerating retreat of European glaciers, which scientists say is primarily driven by human-caused global heating, has revealed a vast array of relics, ancient ecosystems and human remains in recent decades.

In 2015, a barracks where Italian troops had sheltered while fighting the Austro-Hungarian army during the White war – a battle waged across Alpine terrain during the first world war – was discovered on Mount Scorluzzo, a peak overlooking the Stelvio pass. The bodies of dozens of soldiers, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice in the past 20 years.

The most extraordinary discovery of human remains on a melting glacier was made in 1991 when two German hikers found the 5,300-year-old mummified body of a hunter in the Ötztal Alps, close to Italy’s border with Austria. The body of “Ötzi the Iceman”, replete with tattoos, is on display at a museum in Bolzano.

retrieval.retrieval_query: In what year did Paul D MacLean introduce the triune brain model?

results.text:
Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity.

Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts.

citation.title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

results.text:
So, what is it about MacLean’s model that we just can’t seem to let go of? Well, as we’ve seen, people really do seem to love threes. But perhaps there’s more to it than that. The triune brain tells us an ego-stroking story about our place in the world: that we really are the pinnacle of evolution, standing apart from other species. It reaffirms heady ideas about our sovereignty over nature, and tells a reassuring story about our logical, orderly, almost computational abilities. We are storytelling creatures, of course, but this is a story that needs updating – to one about how much in common we have with other animals, and how simplistic assumptions about the way our minds work are almost never true.

• Dr Hannah Critchlow is a neuroscientist and author of The 21st Century Brain (Torva).

Seven Deadly Sins by Guy Leschziner (William Collins,£20)

How Emotions are Made by Lisa Feldman Barrett (Pan, £12.99)

Our Brains, Our Selves by Masud Husain (Canongate, £20)

citation.title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

results.text:
Human behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Frayed tempers, impulsive acts and short termism were signs of the lizard brain winning out. The notion of reptilian impulses “breaking through” proved so popular it found its way into the worlds of pop psychology, business and self-help, and has proved remarkably tenacious. A mini-industry of books, talks and training grew up around the idea that you could draw on the power of the neomammalian brain to keep basic, unhelpful or destructive emotions in check.

The underpinning analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists. It’s easy to grasp, sure, and tells a compelling story. But evolution just doesn’t bolt-on neatly divisible mental capacities in this way.

citation.title: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

results.text:
Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain.

Related: Is culture alive?

retrieval.retrieval_query: In Lisa Feldman Barrett’s account, what does the brain do to keep us alive instead of pitting instinct against reason?

results.text:
As Guy Leschziner, consultant neurologist at London’s Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital put it to me: “the concept of different parts of the brain having different functions is extremely well established. However, to portray humans as having different brain layers, for example a ‘lizard brain’ underlying basic physiological functions, is not borne out by evolutionary or physiological evidence. For a start, mammals and reptiles split early in evolutionary terms. Whilst it is true that more primitive functions in our brains evolved earlier in the course of life on Earth, this view of three separate brain systems driving our basic instincts, emotions and logic respectively does not stack up.”

Lisa Feldman Barrett, professor of psychology at Northeastern University is another contemporary voice actively debunking the lizard brain myth. In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements.

This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun.

This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year.

Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling.

The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet.

We turn our attention this week to one of the sky’s smallest constellations. High overhead from the UK after darkness falls, Lyra, the lyre, is easy to find thanks to the brilliant white star of Vega.

The chart shows the view facing south and looking up towards the zenith from London at 22:30 BST on 17 August.

The September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September.

It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky.

As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal.

This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox.

A near total lunar eclipse will be visible across large swathes of North and South America on Thursday night with millions of people expected to be able to see one of nature’s marvels.

Lunar eclipses occur when Earth moves between the sun and the moon and its shadow is cast on to the lunar surface. In Thursday night’s event 96% of the moon will be darkened by the Earth’s shadow at its peak moment.

The eclipse will be one known as a “blood moon”, as the Earth’s shadow will appear to be reddish due to the way sunlight is scattered by the Earth’s atmosphere. It will mainly be visible in the Americas but also in a few parts of Europe and Africa. It will begin about 9.23pm EST, peaking around 10.33pm EST.

Earlier this month, millions of people across Europe watched a more dramatic solar eclipse where the moon blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness.

The annual Orionid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, offering the chance to see fragments of the most famous comet of all streaking across the night sky.

The Orionids occur every October as Earth passes through a stream of dust left behind by Halley’s comet. As these tiny particles plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at about 66 kilometres per second, they heat the surrounding air and produce the fleeting streaks of light that we call meteors.

This year, the shower is expected to reach its peak during the night of 21–22 October. Under ideal conditions, observers may see between 10 and 20 Orionid meteors per hour. Unfortunately, conditions this year are not ideal because of the presence of a bright waxing gibbous Moon. This will drown out many of the fainter meteors.

Nevertheless, conditions improve during the early hours of the morning. The moon sets at about 03:00 BST, leaving a few hours of darker sky before dawn, just as Orion is climbing high into the sky. Find a safe location with as wide a view of the heavens as possible and simply watch with the naked eye.

The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain.

Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.

The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).

The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists.

In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off.

Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more.

The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly.

Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse.

The Nobel prize in physics 2026 has been awarded to a researcher who turned an enormous block of ice at the south pole into a detector for ghostly particles called neutrinos that reach Earth from outer space.

Prof Francis Halzen, a Belgian particle physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, led work on the IceCube neutrino observatory, which made the first detection of high-energy extraterrestrial neutrinos in 2013, soon after it was switched on.

To build the observatory, scientists, technicians and engineers embedded thousands of basketball-sized light detectors into a cubic kilometre of ice to detect faint flashes of light that can result when neutrinos from space crash into atomic nuclei.

Announcing the prize on Tuesday, the Nobel committee said Halzen won “for decisive contributions to the IceCube neutrino observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”. He receives a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).

He was then kitted out with light-stimulating goggles that captured pictures of the world around him and converted them into single-wavelength images that were projected on to his retina using pulses of light.

Prof Botond Roska, the director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel who co-led the study, welcomed the announcement of the Nobel laureates.

“This is truly wonderful news. I hope this helps to boost all efforts on optogenetic vision restoration to bring back vision to blind patients,” he said.

results.text:
A tiny alga has helped show how memories, feelings and behaviour form in our brains, in research by three scientists awarded the Nobel prize for physiology or medicine this month.

Chlamydomonas is a one-celled alga that swims towards light using a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, remarkably similar to the rhodopsin in our eyes. When the channelrhodopsin detects light, electrically charged ions rush into the cell from outside, triggering an electrical signal incredibly fast that tells the alga to move with its hair-like motor.

In the research, the gene for the Chlamydomonas channelrhodopsin was transferred into living animal brain cells and flashes of light were used to switch individual neurons on or off, helping pinpoint the exact circuits in the brain that control behaviour, feelings, memories, movements, waking and sleeping, and other bodily functions. It could even switch on how mice gather their young in a nest or groom them.

results.text:
Jonathan Levin, the president of Stanford University, said the subsequent discoveries by Deisseroth, along with those of his fellow laureates, have deepened understanding of neural circuits and how they shape feelings, behaviour, and more.

“Their implications are profound, not only for understanding the human brain, but for opening possibilities into new treatments for neurological and psychiatric disorders,” he said.

The work had its origins in research by Hegemann, who wanted to explore how a green alga called Chlamydomonas swam towards light. “He discovered that its eye spot contains a light-sensitive protein that converts light almost instantly into an electrical signal, allowing the alga to move,” said Abdel El Manira, a professor of neuroscience at the Karolinska Institute and member of the Nobel assembly.

Nagel and Hegemann identified the proteins, called channelrhodopsins, and working with frog egg cells they revealed that when the proteins were exposed to blue light, they allowed charged particles – or ions – to flow into the cell, producing an electrical impulse.

results.text:
Further work by the pair revealed that when the genetic instructions for one of the proteins were inserted into human or mouse kidney cells, those cells became light sensitive.

Deisseroth took the discovery even further, using rats to demonstrate that by introducing the gene for a channelrhodopsin into nerve cells, it was possible to produce electrical signals in them using light.

He and his colleagues later applied the approach to nerve cells in the motor cortex of the brains of mice, allowing them to use light – delivered by tiny optic fibres passed through their skull – to trigger movement in the rodent’s whiskers.

Subsequent work in mice showed the approach could also be used to investigate which networks of nerve cells were involved in the formation of particular memories, including fear.

While rooted in basic science, the team’s work has already had real-world implications, opening up a field of medicine known as optogenetic therapy.

In one trial it was used to partially restore the sight of a man who went blind as a result of retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that results in damage to light-sensitive cells in the retina.

The Nobel prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has been awarded to three scientists for their work investigating the mysteries of the brain.

Karl Deisseroth of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of the Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg have been awarded the prize “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”.

The Nobel assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, announced the winners on Monday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).

The 2026 award is the 117th time the prize has been given. Of the 235 laureates – including the latest winners – only 14 have been women and none have been awarded to black scientists.

In a nutshell the trio’s research led to the development of a light-sensitive switch that can be used to control nerve cells in the living brain, switching them on or off.

It’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards.

Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”.

On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners.

Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.

Robert Hall of Stanford University, California, and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, New York, were recognised for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, giving policymakers better tools to smooth out the peaks and troughs of their economies.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).

Related: Nobel prize for economics awarded to two Americans, Hall and Woodford, for work on New Keynesian models – business live

“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.

Can fish and chip shops survive? ‘We made more money by closing than staying open’

The menu is classic: haddock and chips for £11.95, cod and chips a pound more, sides like curry sauce and mushy peas, a few non-fish options. And the food is everything you’d want it to be: the fish fresh and succulent, the batter crisp and light, the chips hot and sog-free. At the end of the shift, Gavin tells me they’ve done about 650 portions that night. The award has raised their profile. They’ve just returned from a trip to see the fishing in Iceland, he says, and they’re about to go to Japan, where they’re doing pop-up stores in three cities. “There’s been so many opportunities – that’s kept us stimulated and excited.” They’re also looking at opening a branch in London, Aman says: “We want to bring the best of the north to the south.” Related: Curb the cod, park the prawns: top chefs on how to swap out the ‘big five’ seafood Despite the union-jack-waving seaside cliches, what makes fish and chips quintessentially British is that it’s interwoven with our history of immigration and internationalism, says Aman, whose family has Punjabi roots.

The ‘Godzilla’ of weight-loss drugs could help improve blood sugar levels, reduce inflammation and cut a person’s body weight by a quarter, according to the largest study of its kind. Unlike other drugs such as Wegovy, which primarily targets the GLP-1 pathway to suppress appetite, or Mounjaro, which contains GLP-1 plus GIP to control blood sugar levels, retatrutide also engages the glucagon receptor, which helps increase energy expenditure. The drug has not yet been approved by any regulatory agency. The red planet, Mars, sails through the beautiful cluster of stars known as the Beehive this week. Catalogued as Messier 44, the cluster lies in the constellation Cancer. ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity

To the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the lively Gaelic heritage centre that records the many centuries of community life on the island. This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spread Christianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history. A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.

citation.title: ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity

results.text:
‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity

Their “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west. Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers

From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries. A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements. The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment. “It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.” One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785. Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table.

The accelerating retreat of European glaciers, which scientists say is primarily driven by human-caused global heating, has revealed a vast array of relics, ancient ecosystems and human remains in recent decades. In 2015, a barracks where Italian troops had sheltered while fighting the Austro-Hungarian army during the White war – a battle waged across Alpine terrain during the first world war – was discovered on Mount Scorluzzo, a peak overlooking the Stelvio pass. The bodies of dozens of soldiers, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice in the past 20 years. The most extraordinary discovery of human remains on a melting glacier was made in 1991 when two German hikers found the 5,300-year-old mummified body of a hunter in the Ötztal Alps, close to Italy’s border with Austria. The body of “Ötzi the Iceman”, replete with tattoos, is on display at a museum in Bolzano.

Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

Humans have a cognitive quirk for the number three. Think of the many stories that use it, from The Three Little Pigs to Goldilocks and the Three Bears and The Three Musketeers. Public information and political campaigns use it for impact and ease of recall (“Stop, look and listen”; “See it. Say it. Sorted”; “Reduce, reuse, recycle”). And then there are psychological or philosophical frameworks: Freud with his id, ego and superego; Plato’s three parts of the human soul; the Holy Trinity. Well, it turns out neuroscience isn’t immune from tri-mania. In 1959 Paul D MacLean set out a new way of thinking about the evolution and function of the brain, which he christened the “triune” – three-in-one – model. It quickly became one of best known and most enduring concepts in human biology. His idea was that a trio of distinct brains are layered inside our skulls, one on top of the other, all fighting to generate our feelings and thoughts. Deep inside, at the centre, lurks the primitive lizard brain, retained from an ancestor we share with reptiles.

In her view, rather than operating as a battleground between ancient instinct, raw emotion and sophisticated logic, the brain is a dynamic, integrated system, whose aim is to keep us alive by predicting and budgeting our energy requirements. Neuroanatomically and behaviourally, if not yet in the popular consciousness, the idea that we all have a lizard brain has been thoroughly discredited. Yet despite the mounting evidence, and the success of more recent frameworks, the triune brain endures. Shockingly, it is still being widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks (as one journal article mischievously titled “Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside” showed). The study also highlighted some of the pitfalls of allowing the hypothesis to go unchallenged, which include giving students a false sense of how evolution unfolds, and promoting the idea that human beings have a monopoly on “rational” actions such as deferring gratification – sacrificing a short-term reward for a longer-term gain. This contains ancient regions responsible for survival, helping us to hunt and forage, and driving our sexual impulses so that we reproduce. A second layer sits wrapped around the first, the so-called mammalian brain. It contains the limbic system, deemed to be the seat of our emotions. It enabled mammals to play, care for and nurse their young and communicate in some crude way. The third and final layer, sheathing all of this and making humans in particular a cut above, is the “neomammalian” brain: the eminently rational cortex. This, it was proposed, provides us with our superior intellect, capacity for language and ability to reason. According to MacLean, it helped to keep in check our primitive, lizard-like impulses and rudimentary emotional reactions. The analogy – of an onion-like brain made up of different strata – is now considered deeply misleading by neurobiologists Human behaviour was thought to be a result of interactions between all three layers of the triune brain. Starwatch: how to spot Saturn as it makes it closest approach to Earth this year

This week offers an excellent opportunity to track down Saturn. The giant planet, situated about 10 times further from the sun than the Earth, reached opposition on 4 October. In this configuration, Earth is passing almost directly between the planet and the sun. This makes opposition an excellent time to see a planet: the distant world rises as the sun sets, remains visible throughout the night and sets around sunrise. It is also at about its closest point to Earth for the year. Saturn is easily visible to the naked eye, looking like a moderately bright, creamy-white object. Unlike most stars, however, its light remains steady rather than noticeably twinkling. The chart shows the view looking east- south-east from London at 2100 BST on 5 October. By this time, Saturn is already well clear of the horizon and will continue climbing higher as the evening progresses. It lies beneath the Great Square of Pegasus, which provides a distinctive signpost to the planet. Saturn is currently shining at about magnitude +0.3. Once you have identified it, try returning to it on subsequent evenings.

Starwatch: Mercury to reach farthest point from the sun

This week offers one of the better opportunities of the year to catch a glimpse of the solar system’s innermost world. Trapped in its small orbit, Mercury never strays far from the sun, meaning it is usually lost to the light of dawn or dusk. On Sunday, however, the planet reached its greatest western elongation, meaning it appeared at its greatest apparent distance from the sun in the morning sky. The next few mornings offer one of the best opportunities this year for catching a glimpse of the planet as it steadily brightens, improving the contrast with the gathering dawn. An early start and an unobstructed view towards the east-north-east will be essential to making the sighting. The chart shows the view looking in this direction from London at 04.30 BST on Tuesday. If your line of sight is free from obstructions, the planet will become visible about a handspan above the horizon some time between 04.30 and 05.00. Binoculars can help, but exercise caution: sunrise on Tuesday from London occurs at 05.28, so stop using binoculars well before this time to protect your eyesight.

Starwatch: Mars signposts the beautiful Beehive cluster

The red planet, Mars, sails through the beautiful cluster of stars known as the Beehive this week. Catalogued as Messier 44, the cluster lies in the constellation Cancer. It has been known since antiquity, when its hazy appearance earned it the Latin name Praesepe, meaning a manger or crib. Although it is one of the brightest star clusters in the night sky, it can be surprisingly difficult to locate because Cancer contains no bright stars to guide the eye towards it. Thankfully, this week Mars acts as the signpost. The chart shows the view looking east from London at 0200 BST on 13 October. Mars will appear as a moderately bright, distinctly red-looking object. Once you have Mars in your sights, look carefully around the planet. From a dark location, the Beehive will appear as a faint, misty patch very close to Mars. Light pollution will make the cluster much harder to see, and wherever you are observing, make sure you allow sufficient time for your eyes to adjust to the dark. This can take about 20 minutes, so resist the temptation to look at the bright screen of your phone.

Near total lunar eclipse will be seen from North and South America Thursday night

A near total lunar eclipse will be visible across large swathes of North and South America on Thursday night with millions of people expected to be able to see one of nature’s marvels. Lunar eclipses occur when Earth moves between the sun and the moon and its shadow is cast on to the lunar surface. In Thursday night’s event 96% of the moon will be darkened by the Earth’s shadow at its peak moment. The eclipse will be one known as a “blood moon”, as the Earth’s shadow will appear to be reddish due to the way sunlight is scattered by the Earth’s atmosphere. It will mainly be visible in the Americas but also in a few parts of Europe and Africa. It will begin about 9.23pm EST, peaking around 10.33pm EST. Earlier this month, millions of people across Europe watched a more dramatic solar eclipse where the moon blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness.

Starwatch: Autumnal equinox in northern hemisphere, spring in the south

The September or autumnal equinox takes place this week. It marks the astronomical beginning of autumn in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere. This year, the precise moment of the equinox falls at 01.05 BST on 23 September. It is commonly said the equinox is when day and night are equal, because the name derives from the Latin for “equal night”, but in practice that is not quite true. An equinox occurs when the sun crosses the celestial equator, the imaginary projection of Earth’s equator into the sky. As Earth moves around its orbit, the sun’s apparent position shifts north and south of the celestial equator. At the equinox it crosses from one side to the other. But even then, day and night are not precisely equal. This is because the sun appears as a disc rather than a point of light, and the bending of its rays by our atmosphere means we can still see it even when it is just below the horizon. Together, these effects make the measured daytime several minutes longer than 12 hours at the equinox.

A tiny alga has helped show how memories, feelings and behaviour form in our brains, in research by three scientists awarded the Nobel prize for physiology or medicine this month. Chlamydomonas is a one-celled alga that swims towards light using a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, remarkably similar to the rhodopsin in our eyes. When the channelrhodopsin detects light, electrically charged ions rush into the cell from outside, triggering an electrical signal incredibly fast that tells the alga to move with its hair-like motor. In the research, the gene for the Chlamydomonas channelrhodopsin was transferred into living animal brain cells and flashes of light were used to switch individual neurons on or off, helping pinpoint the exact circuits in the brain that control behaviour, feelings, memories, movements, waking and sleeping, and other bodily functions. It could even switch on how mice gather their young in a nest or groom them.

Chlamydomonas is a one-celled alga that swims towards light using a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, remarkably similar to the rhodopsin in our eyes.
